title: Golden sets
point: A golden set is a versioned, stratified collection of real cases labelled against a written rubric, grown from every incident, with a held-out split that tuning never sees.
definition: A golden set is the fixed collection of cases an agent is scored against. It is drawn from real traffic and incidents, stratified by task type and difficulty, labelled against a written rubric and versioned like code.

objective.text: Given a sample of production traffic and an incident log, design a stratified, versioned golden set with a held-out split, and state how it grows.

misconceptions.claim: A few dozen hand-written examples make a good golden set.
misconceptions.correction: Invented examples reflect what the team imagines, not what users send. Draw cases from real traffic and incidents, and stratify them so rare but costly task types are represented.

misconceptions.claim: Tuning the prompt until the whole golden set passes proves the change is better.
misconceptions.correction: Repeated tuning against the same cases overfits to them. Keep a held-out split that is never used while tuning, and report the score on it.

l1: Cases come from real traffic and incidents. Every incident or wrong answer becomes a regression case, so the same failure cannot ship twice unnoticed.
The set is stratified across task types and difficulty. A random sample would be mostly easy password resets and almost no complex refunds.
Each case is labelled against a written rubric, and the set is versioned. A score is only comparable with another score on the same version.
l2: Take a support agent whose traffic is 50 per cent account questions, 30 per cent billing, 15 per cent technical and 5 per cent refunds. A 400-case random sample holds only about 20 refunds.
Stratify instead: 100 cases per task type, each split into easy, medium and hard. Refunds now have enough cases for a per-type score to mean something.
Hold out 100 of the 400 cases. Prompt engineers tune on the other 300, and the release report shows the held-out score next to the tuning score.
Last month's incident, where the agent promised a refund outside policy, becomes case 401 in version 1.4, with its label and a link to the incident.
l3: A per-type score needs enough cases to be stable. With 100 cases, a measured 90 per cent has a standard error of about 3 points; with 20 cases it is nearly 7 points.
Golden sets go stale as products and users change. Refresh a share of cases each quarter from recent traffic, but keep incident cases permanently as regression guards.
Version every change to cases, labels or the rubric. When the rubric changes, relabel the affected cases and rescore the baseline, or the comparison is meaningless.
